title: The abbot (ch. 2)
hookLine: the abbot holds the place of Christ and must adapt to each person

lines: ONE NEEDS A PUSH, ONE A JOKE.
cards: Should a good boss treat everyone the same? It sounds like fairness: same rules, same tone, same speech for the whole team. But a coach who barks at every player the same way loses some of them.
One needs a push. One needs a joke. One needs to be left alone until Thursday.
Saint Benedict's Rule has a chapter on the person in charge of the monastery, and it asks something harder than sameness.

teach.b: Chapter two starts high. The abbot is believed to hold the place of Christ in the monastery, because he's called by Christ's own name for the Father: abba.

Benedict points to Paul, who says in the Douay-Rheims that we have received a spirit "whereby we cry: Abba (Father)." So abbot, in the Rule's own words, is a father's name. Then the chapter turns the weight around.

Because he holds that place, the abbot will answer to God for every soul in his care. He's to teach more by what he does than by what he says. He's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery.
And he has to fit himself to each person: their character, their understanding.
Coax one. Correct another. Reason with a third.
Some respond to a gentle word; others need it said plainly. He should serve many temperaments, the Rule says, so that none of the flock is lost. Notice what Benedict isn't saying.
The rules don't change for favorites.
The same care wears different clothes for different people.
Every monk gets the abbot's full attention, not the same speech. The Rule knows it's hard, calling the role difficult and demanding work: ruling souls.
A father's name, a heavy account, and a habit of looking at each face before speaking.

how: In Benedictine monasteries the monks elect their abbot or abbess, who leads the community and is responsible for each member's care, following chapter 2 of the Rule.

o: a bishop who oversees several monasteries
the oldest monk, chosen by seniority alone
the father of a monastery, named from abba

s: the Rule tells the abbot to treat every monk exactly alike
it tells him to fit himself to each person's character and understanding.
the Rule links the abbot's name to abba, father
pointing to Paul: whereby we cry, Abba (Father).
the abbot may put freeborn monks ahead of the rest
the Rule says he's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery.

games.q: you're the abbot. one monk needs a firm word, another is easily crushed. what does the Rule ask of you?
o: give both the same firm speech.
fit yourself to each: correct one, coax the other.
games.why: the Rule asks the abbot to adapt to each temperament, so that none of the flock is lost.

practice: Bring to mind two people you look after, work with or live with, and picture them side by side.
Ask what each needs from you right now: maybe one needs a push and the other gentleness, one more words and the other fewer, and just let their two faces be different.
If you pray, ask God for the wisdom to care for each of them as they are.

wordCard.voice: Abbot. The father of a monastery, named, the Rule says, from abba, who holds the place of Christ and must fit himself to each person in his care. Today's word.

orig.note: an Aramaic word for father, kept in the Greek of Romans 8:15; the Rule gives it as the abbot's name.

carryVoice: Your line: each one differently. Every face gets full attention, if not the same words. See you tomorrow.
